title: The Stand-Up Exercise to Illustrate Shared Values and Experiences
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece describes a concrete facilitation exercise leaders can use to visibly demonstrate a team's shared values rather than merely asserting them. The technique involves a facilitator posing a graduated series of statements -- each broader than the last -- asking people to stand when the statement applies to them, until the entire room is standing together by the final statement. A worked example around client-service values shows how the escalating statements build toward universal agreement, which the leader can then use as a springboard to name the group's shared commitments. The essay notes the exercise also works in reverse (sit-down) and remains impactful even for people who've encountered similar exercises before.
points: The exercise uses a graduated series of statements, asking people to stand when each applies to them, building toward the whole room standing together.
A worked example around client and customer service shows how three escalating statements bring an entire audience to its feet.
Once everyone is standing, the leader has a natural forum to name the shared values and commitments the moment just demonstrated.
The exercise can also run in reverse as a sit-down, with the audience starting up and sitting as each statement applies to them.
Demonstrating unity through a visible, participatory moment tends to land more powerfully than simply asserting it verbally.
quotes: It is important for leaders to remind the team that what they share in common is much more powerful than what separates them.
The idea is to pose a successive list of statements, asking audience members to stand up when they agree, until everyone is out of their seats because of what they share in common.
If what you do for clients and customers seriously matters to you and you are committed to delighting them through your actions, please stand up.
By the third statement and request to rise, everyone in the room will be standing.
Leaders can also employ the metaphor of "standing together in unity" to reinforce other messages tied to clients and customers in this example.
When it comes to emphasizing group cohesion, demonstrating unity rather than just saying it can be the best call.
